headings: Built to be used by everyone.
pages.text: Accessibility statement · Innovent Accessibility Built to be used by everyone. What we have done on this site for people who browse with assistive technology, what we have not finished, and where to send a problem. Statement dated 19 September 2026 · Applies to innovent.io Our commitment Innovent wants innovent.io to be usable by everyone, whatever tools they browse with. We work to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Level AA , and we treat the gaps listed below as defects to fix, not as acceptable exceptions. What is in place today A "Skip to content" link as the first focusable element on every page, and a single main landmark per page. Every navigation region is labelled, and every menu control is a real button or link with a visible name. Text alternatives on every meaningful image, including the product screenshots and partner logos. All motion on the site — the animated diagrams, counters, carousels and map sweeps — is stilled when your system asks for reduced motion, and the same content is shown without it. Structured headings and structured data on every page so screen readers and search engines read the same outline you see. Colour is never the only carrier of meaning: status is always also written in words. Known gaps We would rather list these than claim a conformance level we have not earned. Some captions and labels in the product mock-ups are set below 14px; we are raising these where they carry information rather than texture. A number of footer links and small controls fall short of the 44×44px touch target guideline on phones. The mega menu on desktop is built on the client and is not yet fully operable with the keyboard alone. We have not yet completed a formal third-party audit or published a VPAT / Accessibility Conformance Report. Public-sector buyers who need one for Section 508 or EN 301 549 can ask for our current self-assessment. Tell us what is broken If any part of this site is hard to use, write to info@innovent.io with the page address and what you were trying to do. We reply within two business days and we fix what we can in the next release. The Innfini platform This statement covers the public website only. Accessibility of the Innfini platform itself is addressed in each customer's contract and in the platform documentation, which is available to customers and prospective customers on request.

headings: Abu Dhabi Ports: 280,000 containers, one operating layer
pages.text: Abu Dhabi Ports: 280,000 containers, one operating layer · Innovent CUSTOMER April 2026 9 min read Abu Dhabi Ports: 280,000 containers, one operating layer SA S. Al-Mahmoud · Innovent · Engineering AD Ports Group runs one of the busiest port complexes in the Middle East. Containers move through six terminals. Cold-chain freight ages in real time. Suppliers, contractors, and last-mile carriers coordinate around the clock. None of that was easy when each system lived on its own. The starting point When we walked the site, AD Ports was running 14 separate systems for what should have been one workflow. The TOS didn't know what the yard hostlers were doing. The cold-chain loggers reported to a vendor portal. Supplier scheduling lived in email. Each gate had its own paper checklist. What we changed Innfini deployed as the enterprise digital-operations platform — reading from every existing system through pre-built connectors, writing back through the same fabric. The TOS still ran. The cold-chain hardware stayed. What changed is that they finally talked to each other. Warehousing and logistics surfaced through one console. Cold-chain temperature alerts arrived in seconds, not at delivery. Supplier portals replaced email threads. Last-mile fleet telemetry meant ETAs customers could plan against. Result Port-wide visibility. 24/7 cold-chain integrity. Streamlined supplier coordination. The operations director told us "we have one operating picture for the first time." The lessons Two things mattered. First: we didn't ask AD Ports to rip and replace anything. The existing systems work — they just weren't connected. Innfini's connector layer was the entire reason this deployment shipped in months instead of years. Second: visibility isn't the same as automation. The first six months were about making operations visible. The next twelve are about making them automatic. Agentic dispatch, predictive cold-chain interventions, and automated supplier coordination are next.

pages.title: Why agentic AI breaks in production — and how we fixed it
pages.description: Most agentic AI demos work brilliantly until they hit production. We learned this the hard way running goal-driven agents inside Civil Defense.
headings: Why agentic AI breaks in production — and how we fixed it
pages.text: Why agentic AI breaks in production — and how we fixed it · Innovent ENGINEERING May 2026 12 min read Why agentic AI breaks in production — and how we fixed it KP Dr. K. Patel · Innovent · Engineering Most agentic AI demos work brilliantly until they hit production. We learned this the hard way running goal-driven agents inside Civil Defense, police forces, and chemical plants. The failure modes are predictable. The fixes are unglamorous. Here's what three years of deployment taught us. The first failure: tool hallucination When an LLM picks a tool that doesn't exist, you don't find out until production. Schema-strict tool registries prevent this — every tool has a typed signature, and the planner can only emit calls that match. We rejected pure function-calling APIs in favor of typed action grammars that the planner generates against, not in spite of. Lesson If your agent framework lets the LLM invent tool names, you don't have a framework. You have a chatbot with extra steps. The second failure: policy drift Approval policies that live in prompt text decay. The model summarizes them, paraphrases them, eventually forgets them. We moved every policy into structural guardrails — code that runs after the model proposes an action and before the system executes it. The model can't bypass what isn't in its execution path. The third failure: multi-agent gridlock When two agents share a workspace, they fight. We watched a dispatch agent and a maintenance agent argue over the same vehicle for 14 minutes in a staging environment. The fix isn't smarter coordination — it's explicit lock acquisition in the object graph. Whoever holds the lock wins. Conflicts surface as events, not as silent races. The fourth failure: silent regression Agents drift. Last quarter's "good enough" model becomes this quarter's liability. We run shadow agents on every production decision — the live agent acts, the shadow agent predicts. When divergence crosses threshold, the shadow gets promoted or the live agent gets retrained. A production agent isn't a model. It's a model, a typed action grammar, structural policy, lock-protected state, and shadow evaluation — together. Anything less and you're running a demo. What we won't do anymore Prompt-only policy enforcement. Unbounded tool registries. Shared mutable state without locks. Trusting demo performance. None of this is novel computer science. All of it is the difference between an agent that works in a demo and an agent that runs Dubai Police's critical-asset chain-of-custody.

pages.title: Air-gapped Innfini: the engineering trade-offs
pages.description: Federal and defense environments demand air-gapped deployment. The cloud is not an option. The internet is not an option.
pages.text: Air-gapped Innfini: the engineering trade-offs · Innovent SECURITY March 2026 11 min read Air-gapped Innfini: the engineering trade-offs AV A. Volkov · Innovent · Engineering Federal and defense environments demand air-gapped deployment. The cloud is not an option. The internet is not an option. Even DNS resolution to external hosts can be a non-starter. We've built Innfini to run in these environments. Here's what changes. What still works Most of Innfini doesn't care about the internet. The object graph, the event backbone, the connector layer, the edge runtime — all of these operate on local infrastructure. The model gateway can serve pre-deployed models locally. Agentic orchestration runs entirely on-prem. What needs different patterns Model updates Models can't pull from a remote model registry. Updates ship as signed artifacts through air-gapped media. We support the oras OCI artifact format for this — the same patterns federal agencies already use for container distribution. License validation License keys must validate without phoning home. We use offline cryptographic license tokens with limited time-to-live and rotation through the same air-gap media channel. Telemetry No telemetry leaves the air-gapped boundary. Operational telemetry is captured locally and can be exported on customer request through the same secure channels. The hard part It isn't any one technical change. It's the operational discipline of every team treating "the internet doesn't exist" as a first-class constraint, not an afterthought. What you give up Continuous improvement loops slow down. The platform updates on the customer's cadence, not ours. Model retraining requires customer-side ground truth. The trade-off is sovereignty — and for the customers who need it, it's the only option that exists.

pages.title: Camera-to-RFID fusion: a practitioner's guide
pages.description: Cameras see well. RFID counts well. Each lies in its own way. The interesting work in industrial computer vision isn't about either sensor alone.
pages.text: Camera-to-RFID fusion: a practitioner's guide · Innovent RESEARCH April 2026 18 min read Camera-to-RFID fusion: a practitioner's guide MC M. Chen · Innovent · Engineering Cameras see well. RFID counts well. Each lies in its own way. The interesting work in industrial computer vision isn't about either sensor alone — it's about fusing them so the lies cancel out. Here's how we do it in production. Why neither alone is enough RFID gives you "this tag is in this zone" with near-perfect counts but no spatial information beneath the antenna footprint. Vision gives you precise positions but is blind to occluded objects, mistakes carbon-fiber for steel, and breaks under shift-changing light. Fusion is where the magic happens. The camera tells you where ; the RFID tells you what . Together you get item-level position tracking that beats either modality alone. The pipeline In production, our pipeline runs four stages — detection, association, fusion, and reconciliation. Each has its own failure modes. Stage 1: Detection A fine-tuned YOLO-class model identifies object candidates in each frame. We train per site because lighting, angles, and object classes are too varied for a generic model. Stage 2: Association RFID reads are timestamped. Vision detections are timestamped. We associate them using a Hungarian-algorithm-style assignment that considers spatial proximity, RFID signal strength, and time alignment. Stage 3: Fusion Once associated, an Kalman-filter tracks each object's position across frames. RFID updates anchor the track to identity. Vision updates refine the position. Stage 4: Reconciliation A nightly job reconciles the day's tracks against ground truth — manual cycle counts, ERP records, or the next-day reality. Drift gets fed back into retraining. Calibration tip The biggest source of error in fusion is RFID antenna placement. Spend a week walking the site with a calibration cart before you trust any model. We see 99%+ match accuracy in production on yard operations. That number breaks if the antenna placement breaks, if the camera angles change, or if a new SKU enters without retraining. Maintenance discipline matters more than model architecture.

pages.title: Civic AI under sunlight: how we publish every decision
pages.description: Civic AI is on the receiving end of an accountability conversation that enterprise AI never had to have.
headings: Civic AI under sunlight: how we publish every decision
pages.text: Civic AI under sunlight: how we publish every decision · Innovent POLICY March 2026 14 min read Civic AI under sunlight: how we publish every decision LR L. Robles · Innovent · Engineering Civic AI is on the receiving end of an accountability conversation that enterprise AI never had to have. When a permit gets denied or a 911 call gets prioritized, the public deserves to understand why. The good news is the engineering is straightforward. The hard work is institutional. The transparency stack Innfini for cities ships with a transparency stack that runs alongside every agent. Three layers: Decision registers — every algorithmic action recorded with its inputs, outputs, and reasoning. Equity dashboards — outcomes broken down by district, demographic, and time. Public-facing. Appeal workflows — residents can challenge any algorithmic decision through a structured intake. What gets published Every decision that affects a resident's services, permits, or access is logged with: the algorithm version, the input features, the output, the confidence, and an explanation in plain language. The log is queryable by anyone via a public API. Why this matters Black-box civic AI is a political liability waiting to happen. Cities that ship transparent decisions don't get caught flat-footed when the press starts asking questions. The hard part: equity audits Decision registers are easy. Equity audits are hard. The question "is this AI fair?" doesn't have one answer — it has dozens, and different ones matter to different communities. We work with each city's civil-rights office to define which fairness metrics get tracked and surfaced. The platform doesn't pick fairness for you. It instruments it. The choice — and the conversation — stays with the public.

pages.title: Sub-100ms decisions at the edge — without a GPU
pages.description: A GPU at every edge site is a non-starter at scale. Multiply $5,000+ per site by 100+ sites and the economics collapse.
headings: Sub-100ms decisions at the edge — without a GPU
pages.text: Sub-100ms decisions at the edge — without a GPU · Innovent ENGINEERING February 2026 15 min read Sub-100ms decisions at the edge — without a GPU JP J. Park · Innovent · Engineering A GPU at every edge site is a non-starter at scale. Multiply $5,000+ per site by 100+ sites and the economics collapse. We chose a harder path: production-grade inference on $400 commodity gateways. Here's how it works. The model side Three constraints drive the architecture. First, models must be quantized to int8 or smaller. Second, they must run on CPU. Third, they must fit in 4GB of RAM. The model architecture follows. Vision: MobileNet-v3 backbone with custom heads per use case. Anomaly: lightweight autoencoders with bounded reconstruction error. Forecasting: ESN (echo-state networks) and gradient-boosted trees over deep models. Object detection: int8 YOLOv8n family fine-tuned per site. The runtime side Inference latency on commodity x86 (Atom-class) runs 30–80ms for our vision models. Three patterns get us there: Pattern 1: Frame skipping For continuous vision, we don't need to infer every frame. We infer key frames and interpolate. A 15-FPS camera becomes effectively 5-FPS inference — well within budget. Pattern 2: Cascaded inference A cheap "is something happening?" detector runs always-on. The expensive classifier only fires when the cheap detector triggers. The expensive model effectively runs at 1-FPS. Pattern 3: Edge-local caching Most decisions repeat. An LRU cache on the inference output catches the common case in microseconds. Cache hit rates on retail RFID workloads run 70%+. The honest answer You don't get GPU-class performance on CPU. You get good-enough performance for 90% of edge workloads at 1/10th the per-site cost. That trade-off is what makes the math work.

pages.text: Abu Dhabi Civil Defense: RFID equipment readiness across 10 stations · Innovent ★ Equipment readiness UAE · Federal · Civil Defense RFID equipment readiness for Civil Defense — 10 stations, every asset accounted for. Innovent tagged every piece of firefighting equipment with RFID across 10 Abu Dhabi Civil Defense stations — verifying automatically what is on the truck and what is missing, before and after every mission , and integrating the result with the agency's ERP and readiness platform . 10 Civil Defense stations RFID On every equipment item 2× Checks per mission ERP + readiness platform Challenges The brief 01 Manual equipment checks. Confirming what was loaded on each appliance depended on crews working through paper checklists under time pressure, at the worst possible moment. 02 Equipment lost on the ground. Items left at an incident scene were often only discovered days later, during the next inventory count rather than on return. 03 Readiness could not be evidenced. Asset data in the ERP and operational state in the readiness platform were reconciled by hand, so neither was fully trusted. Solution Innfini as the equipment readiness layer. Innovent tagged every piece of firefighting equipment across 10 stations with RFID and made the appliance itself the reader. Loading an appliance now produces a record rather than a signature: the system knows what is aboard, what is missing and what came back, and writes that state into the agency's ERP and readiness platform without anyone retyping it. RFID asset tagging Every firefighting equipment item carries a rugged RFID tag, registered once against its ERP asset record. On-truck verification The appliance reads its own load, so what is aboard and what is missing is known without a manual count. Pre-mission check Loading produces an automatic readiness record before the appliance leaves the station. Post-mission check On return the same read flags anything not recovered, while the scene is still reachable. ERP integration Asset state, stock levels and maintenance status flow straight into the agency's ERP with no re-entry. Readiness platform Station and appliance readiness is derived from real per-item data rather than declared. A crew leaves the station knowing exactly what is on the truck, and returns knowing exactly what came back — without a clipboard in sight. pages.text: Agentic Orchestration — Plans, Acts, Explains · Innovent Platform · Capabilities Plan · Act · Explain Plan, decide, act, explain — under policy. Goal-driven agents that reason over sensor state, take action in connected systems, and document every step in an audit log. Built for environments where being wrong has a cost. HTN+LLM Hybrid planning <1s Decision latency 100% Auditable Policy Guardrailed Why it matters The problem 01 LLM-only agents break. Pure LLM agents hallucinate, drift, and break at edge cases. The cost of wrong actions in mission-critical environments is too high to leave to fluency. 02 No safety boundaries. Without typed policies, agents can take unauthorized actions. Approval flows are afterthoughts in most frameworks. 03 Black-box decisions. Inexplicable agents are unacceptable in regulated environments. Audit chains require step-by-step provenance. 04 Multi-agent gridlock. When multiple agents share a workspace, they fight. Coordination has to be explicit. What Innfini delivers The capability surface . HTN + LLM planning Hierarchical task networks ground LLM reasoning. The planner knows your operating model; the LLM handles the language. Typed action grammars Models can only emit calls that match a typed signature. Tool hallucination has no surface area. Policy guardrails Typed policies enforce scope, approval thresholds, and rate limits. Agents physically cannot exceed authority. Decision audit ledger Every plan, every tool call, every override recorded with timestamp, identity, and reasoning trace. Multi-agent coordination Agents share state through the object graph. Conflicts surface as events, not silent races. Operator-in-the-loop Configurable approval modes — auto, attended, supervised. Operators see what agents will do before they do it. The loop Six steps, under one second. An agent is not a prompt. Each cycle perceives current state from the graph, plans against your operating model, is checked by policy, acts through typed tool calls, and writes an explanation — every pass, without exception. The policy gate Authority is checked, not assumed. Every proposed action passes a typed policy gate evaluated server-side. Scope, thresholds, rate limits, clearance and reversibility are checked before anything executes — so an agent cannot widen its own authority. Autonomy modes Autonomy is earned per action type. There is no global autonomy switch. Each action type sits at one of four levels, and moves up only after a shadow period proves its precision. Irreversible actions stay advisory permanently. The audit ledger Every cycle leaves a record. One real agent run, written immutably: what it saw, what it planned, what policy said, what it did, and what it held for a human. This is the artefact an inquiry or regulator reads. Multi-agent Agents share state, never messages. Agents coordinate through the object graph rather than talking to each other. Two agents claiming the same object produce a visible conflict event for an operator to arbitrate — not a silent race. Agentic AI for environments where being wrong has a cost. Plan, act, explain — every step under policy, every decision auditable. pages.text: The Operations AI Maturity Model · Innovent White Paper Strategy · white paper Read online PDF in preparation The Operations AI Maturity Model Five stages from "dashboarded" to "agentic." A self-assessment for operations leaders considering an AI-native platform. Get the PDF when it is ready Talk to a solutions architect INNOVENT · WHITE PAPER The Operations AI Maturity Model White paper · PDF in preparation Operations leaders ask us a version of the same question: "are we ready for agentic AI?" The honest answer is "depends on where you are." This paper proposes a maturity model — five stages — to make that question precise. The five stages Stage 1 — Dashboarded. Data is visible. Decisions are manual. The organization can see operations but can't intervene faster than the next standup. Stage 2 — Alerted. Anomaly detection fires. Operators get pinged. The pace of intervention shortens from days to hours. Stage 3 — Recommended. Models propose actions. Operators approve. Decision time compresses to minutes. Cognitive load increases. Stage 4 — Supervised agentic. Agents act under policy with operator approval at thresholds. Routine decisions automate. Operator span of control grows. Stage 5 — Autonomous agentic. Agents act independently within policy. Operators handle exceptions. The operating model is fundamentally different. Self-assessment The paper includes a 30-item self-assessment with scoring guidance. Most operations organizations sit between stages 2 and 3. The interesting question is what it takes to move.
